paras: The expulsion of C. A. Buchanan from West Point, Mississippi, took place in August 1904, when a mob organized at a white mass meeting ordered the Black editor and preacher to close his newspaper office and leave the state. Buchanan moved his paper to Guthrie, Oklahoma, and recounted the episode there in an editorial a year later.

Buchanan was described as "a Negro editor and preacher" who published a newspaper in West Point. According to his later account, the trouble began with an item in his paper advising Black readers not to visit "the St. Louis University campus" because "There is no accommodation for Negroes whatever." White residents treated the item as "advocating social equality."

By Buchanan's account, the white citizens of West Point called a mass meeting at the Court House, organized a mob, and sent it to his office. The mob carried instructions to order him to close the office and leave the state at once with his employees, his family and all his belongings, and he wrote that he "had to do or die." He said the daily papers of the South carried the news on August 27, 1904, under the caption "Move On Orders Given To Negro Preacher."

Buchanan closed down in West Point and resumed issuing "the same sheet" in Guthrie. No report of arrests or of any official response appears in the coverage. In August 1905 the paper noted that "Editor Buchanan" had been invited to move back to Mississippi at the expense of his friends, and answered, "Hold on, boys! Oklahoma is running this thing all right."
The only full account is Buchanan's own, printed in the Oklahoma Safeguard on August 31, 1905, and the Southern daily reports he described do not appear in the coverage.

The Safeguard editorial answered that white Southerners "believe in resentment first and investigation afterwards." It then turned partly against Black leaders, citing John Wanamaker's dinner invitation to Booker T. Washington and warning that leaders who acted this way would "stir up hell by their indiscreet acts."

accounts.label: Victim's own editorial
accounts.gist: A Court House mass meeting of West Point whites organized a mob that ordered Buchanan to close his office and leave the state 'or die' for a travel warning they called advocating social equality.

accounts.label: Southern daily press (as described by Buchanan)
accounts.gist: Ran 'Move On Orders Given To Negro Preacher' on Aug. 27, 1904, saying he was ordered out for advocating social equality; known only through A2.

framing.detail: The Safeguard said white Southerners 'believe in resentment first and investigation afterwards,' but also urged Black leaders to avoid 'indiscreet acts' such as the Wanamaker dinner.
A light item joked that Buchanan was 'invited to move back to Mississippi at the expense of his friends.'

record_check.dossier: The white citizens of West Point, via a Court House mass meeting that organized a mob (Buchanan's account only)
No county named in the papers; only West Point, Miss.
Consistent: Southern dailies ran the story Aug. 27, 1904; the 1905-08-31 issue marked twelve months since closing
Two Safeguard issues mention it (1905-08-03 in passing, 1905-08-31 in full)

info: About August 1904; Southern dailies carried the story on Aug. 27 of the previous year, and the 1905-08-31 issue marked 'just twelve months' since the paper closed in West Point
